newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela reform plan, still much to do after 1 yr.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela reform plan, still much to do after 1 yr.

text.p: One year into its tough program of IMF-sponsored reforms, Venezuela's macroeconomic indicators are shining but government ministers admitted Tuesday the real reforms are yet to come.

"True reform measures are yet to be implemented and those are structural," Trade and Industry Minister Freddy Rojas Parra said in a seminar reviewing the first birthday of the reform package, which is known as the Venezuelan Agenda.

A year ago, a somber President Rafael Caldera reversed populist election promises when he told Venezuelans that interest rates would be freed, exchange rates liberalized, gasoline prices raised fivefold and taxes increased.
The widely-feared social uprising never materialized as the measures quickly hit a population already battered by years of recession that had left eight out of ten below the poverty line.
"A strong social effort was made to help maintain the peace," said Information Fernando Egana, who described at the seminar how a program of directed subsidies had reached 3.5 million families.

Buoyed by a fortunate spike in international oil prices and the IMF seal of approval, foreign reserves soared to over $15 billion, confidence in the economy grew and growth prospects improved as inflation trended downwards to March's 1.6 percent rate -- the lowest in five years.
This year the government expects the economy to grow upwards of four percent, after shrinking 1.6 percent in 1996.
But while the numbers glitter, the macroeconomic bounty is yet to filter down to most Venezuelans, analysts say, and ministers admit much remains to be done.
"The second phase of Venezuelan Agenda is structural reforms," Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar said Tuesday.

An ambitious series of measures are on the slate: the sale of huge aluminum and iron firms; reform of a notoriously corrupt and inefficient judiciary that not only condemns innocents to years of jail but also deters investment; and passage of two macroeconomic funds that will be used to pay-down debt and shield the oil-dependent economy from the lean years of low oil prices.

Congressional approval of crucial social security reforms, already agreed last month in ground-breaking talks with union and private sector leaders, will also free up rigid labor markets, so increasing long term productivity, the analysts say.
"There is more to go, but if you review the year, a lot has been done ... it's quite impressive, and you can't just put it all down to the good luck of high oil prices," one Western diplomat said.

In December the government re-privatised two of the country's largest banks, Banco de Venezuela and Banco Consolidado, and successfully concluded a $1-billion global share offering in telephone company CANTV.

A number of price hikes in public services, mainly electricity, are pending and an increasingly overvalued bolivar used to bear down on inflation in lieu of spending cuts worries many who fear a devaluation crash in the future.
But analysts, albeit grudgingly, give high marks to Caldera for presiding over the reforms after having sworn he would never go on his knees to the IMF.
"He has used politics to pursue policies ... he knows his people well," one foreign investment banker said.
"As for the bolivar, that's a useful price anchor, but it also has its political ends ... its strength helps boost consumption and accelerate the approach of the feel good factor."
